output.title: Why proof-of-concept debt survives
output.body:
Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one boring reason: the pilot solved part of the problem, but nobody owned the last mile of daily use. In a small business, that last mile is where the real cost sits: who watches it, who fixes it, and who keeps it in the workflow once the demo is done.

That is the bounded decision I would look at first. Not “should we use AI everywhere?” but “does this recurring workflow have a clear owner if we automate it?” If the answer is fuzzy, the pilot tends to turn into shelf-ware. That is just debt with nicer phrasing.

For an owner-operator, the comparison is simple: keep paying with time and attention for manual work, or invest in a narrow automation for one repeatable workflow. Bareni’s diagnostic is built around that question. It identifies one recurring workflow, checks honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines scope, fixed price, and measures. Timings and scope are intended, not guaranteed. Finished code and the relevant accounts stay in the customer’s name; there is no separate formal build gate.

A practical next step is to pick one workflow you repeat every week — customer questions, invoice entry, lead routing, or data sync — and ask: once this is automated, who owns running it day to day? If you cannot name that person, the problem is not the model. Clarify that first before building.
